name: Derivatives Pricing & Risk
title: Risk Quant
blurb: Murex and Calypso projects revolve around how swaps, FX forwards and options are priced and risk-managed, so understanding curves, Greeks, VaR and XVA lets Arin talk to traders and risk teams instead of only configuring screens.

chapters.title: Discounting and discount factors
chapters.read: A derivatives or fixed-income textbook's opening chapter on time value of money: simple, annual and continuous compounding, day-count basics (ACT/360, ACT/365), and the discount factor DF(0,T) as the price today of 1 paid at T.
chapters.produce: Build a small spreadsheet that converts one zero rate into discount factors under simple, annual and continuous compounding for maturities from 3 months to 10 years, and plot the three curves.

quiz.q: The 2-year zero rate is 3% with annual compounding. What is the 2-year discount factor? (4 decimal places)
What is the present value of ¥1,000,000 received in 5 years if the continuously compounded rate is 2%?
A 90-day money-market deposit pays 4% simple interest on an ACT/360 basis. What is the 90-day discount factor? (4 decimal places)
The 3-year discount factor is 0.91. What is the continuously compounded 3-year zero rate, in %?
What does the discount factor DF(0,T) represent?
opts: The value today of one unit of currency paid with certainty at time T
The interest rate earned between today and time T
The value at time T of one unit of currency invested today
The probability that a payment due at time T is actually made
quiz.ex: A discount factor converts a future cash flow into today's value; the value at T of 1 invested today is its reciprocal (the growth factor).

quiz.q: Rates are positive at all maturities. Which statement about discount factors must be true?
opts: Discount factors rise as maturity increases
Discount factors fall as maturity increases
Discount factors are greater than 1 for long maturities
Discount factors equal the zero rates for each maturity
quiz.ex: With positive rates, money received later is worth less today, so DF(0,T) decreases in T and stays below 1.

chapters.title: Yield curve bootstrapping and forward rates
chapters.read: The yield-curve construction chapter of a fixed-income or derivatives textbook: deposits, FRAs/futures and par swaps as curve inputs, solving discount factors one maturity at a time, interpolation, and implied forward rates.
chapters.produce: Bootstrap a 5-year annual discount curve in a spreadsheet from one deposit rate and four par swap rates, then compute the 1-year forward rates it implies and check that each input instrument reprices to par.

quiz.q: The 1-year zero rate is 2% (annual compounding). A 2-year par bond pays a 3% annual coupon and is priced at 100. Bootstrap the 2-year discount factor. (4 decimal places)
A curve has DF(2) = 0.9423190, What is the 2-year zero rate with annual compounding, in %?
Annually compounded zero rates are 2% for 1 year and 3% for 2 years. What is the implied 1-year rate starting in 1 year (annual compounding), in %?
DF(1.0) = 0.970 and DF(1.5) = 0.955. What is the simple forward rate for the period from 1.0 to 1.5 years, in %?
Why are curve instruments processed in order of increasing maturity when bootstrapping?
opts: Longer instruments are less liquid, so they are given lower weight
Short rates are always higher, so they must be fixed first
Each new instrument's price depends on discount factors already solved at shorter maturities, leaving one unknown
Regulation requires curves to be published from short to long
quiz.ex: Bootstrapping solves one discount factor per step; all earlier cash flows of the new instrument are discounted with factors found in previous steps.

quiz.q: The zero curve slopes upward. How do 1-year forward rates compare with zero rates of the same end maturity?
opts: Forward rates lie below the zero rates
Forward rates equal the zero rates
Forward rates are always negative
Forward rates lie above the zero rates
quiz.ex: A zero rate is an average of the forwards up to that maturity; if the average is rising, the marginal (forward) rate must be above it.

chapters.title: Pricing an interest rate swap
chapters.read: The interest rate swap chapter of a derivatives textbook plus a vendor or bank primer on OIS swaps: fixed and floating legs, the annuity (PV01), the par swap rate, and valuing a seasoned swap by re-pricing both legs on today's curve.
chapters.produce: Price a 5-year ¥10bn payer swap in a spreadsheet from your bootstrapped curve: leg PVs, par rate, MTM at an off-market fixed rate, and the PV change for a 1bp parallel shift.

quiz.q: Annual discount factors are DF1 = 0.97, DF2 = 0.94, DF3 = 0.91. What is the 3-year par swap rate (annual fixed payments), in %?
Same curve (DF1 0.97, DF2 0.94, DF3 0.91). What is the PV of the fixed leg of a 3-year swap on ¥1bn notional paying 2.5% annually?
Same curve. At inception, what is the PV of the floating leg of a 3-year swap on ¥1bn notional (no exchange of notional)?
Same curve. What is the value to the fixed-rate PAYER of the 3-year ¥1bn swap with a 2.5% fixed rate?
quiz.ex: Payer receives floating, pays fixed: 90,000,000 − 70,500,000 = +¥19,500,000.

quiz.q: A company enters a payer swap (pays fixed, receives floating). When does the swap gain value for the company?
opts: When market swap rates rise after the trade
When market swap rates fall after the trade
Only when the floating index fixes exactly at the fixed rate
Never: a swap always has zero value after inception
quiz.ex: If rates rise, the floating leg received is worth more while the fixed leg paid is unchanged, so the payer gains.

quiz.q: Same curve (annuity 2.82). By how much does the swap's value change if the fixed rate on ¥1bn notional is raised by 1 basis point?

chapters.title: Pricing an FX forward
chapters.read: The currency forwards section of a derivatives or international finance textbook: covered interest parity, forward points, outright forwards versus FX swaps, and how to value an existing forward by discounting the difference to today's forward.
chapters.produce: Build a USD/JPY forward calculator that takes spot and both currencies' rates, outputs outright and forward points for 1M–1Y, and values a seasoned forward contract.

quiz.q: USD/JPY spot is 150.00. 1-year simple rates: JPY 0.5%, USD 5.0%. What is the 1-year outright forward (yen per dollar)? (2 decimals)
USD/JPY spot 150.00. 6-month simple rates (ACT/360 ignored, use T = 0.5): JPY 0.5%, USD 5.0%. What is the 6-month forward? (2 decimals)
From the 1-year example (spot 150.00, forward 143.5714), what are the forward points in yen (forward minus spot)?
quiz.ex: Points = 143.5714 − 150.00 = −6.43 yen: USD trades at a forward discount.

quiz.q: You are long USD 1,000,000 forward at 145.00 maturing in 1 year. Today's 1-year forward is 150 × 1.005/1.05 and the 1-year JPY rate is 0.5% simple. What is the contract's value today in yen?
Under covered interest parity, the currency with the higher interest rate…
opts: trades at a forward premium to its spot value
trades at a forward discount to its spot value
has a forward rate equal to spot
must appreciate in spot terms over the period
quiz.ex: The forward offsets the interest differential; otherwise borrowing low, converting and lending high would be a riskless profit.

quiz.q: What is an FX swap?
opts: A contract exchanging fixed for floating interest in a single currency
An option to exchange currencies at a fixed rate
A spot (or near) exchange of two currencies combined with the reverse exchange at a later date at an agreed forward rate
A single exchange of currencies at a future date with no near leg
quiz.ex: An FX swap has two legs in opposite directions; a single future exchange is an outright forward, and fixed-for-floating in one currency is an interest rate swap.

chapters.title: Black-Scholes, put-call parity and the Greeks
chapters.read: The Black-Scholes-Merton chapter and the Greeks chapter of an options textbook: lognormal stock model, d1 and d2, call and put formulas, put-call parity, and delta, gamma, vega, theta and rho with their intuition for hedging.
chapters.produce: Implement Black-Scholes call/put prices and the five Greeks in a spreadsheet or Python, verify put-call parity numerically, and chart delta and gamma against spot for three expiries.

quiz.q: Black-Scholes inputs: S = 100, K = 100, r = 5% (continuous), σ = 20%, T = 1 year, no dividends. What is the European call price? (2 decimals)
Using put-call parity with the same inputs (call price 10.4506), what is the European put price? (2 decimals)
Same inputs (d1 = 0.35). What is the delta of the call? (3 decimals)
quiz.ex: Call delta = N(d1) = N(0.35) ≈ 0.637.

quiz.q: Same inputs (d1 = 0.35, T = 1). What is the call's vega per 1 volatility point (i.e. per 0.01 of σ)? (3 decimals)
quiz.ex: Vega = S × φ(d1) × √T = 100 × 0.3752 × 1 = 37.52 per unit σ, so 0.375 per vol point.

quiz.q: For a European option, when is gamma typically largest?
opts: When the option is deep in-the-money with long maturity
When the option is deep out-of-the-money close to expiry
Gamma is the same for all strikes and maturities
When the option is at-the-money and close to expiry
quiz.ex: Delta changes fastest around the strike, and that change becomes sharper as expiry approaches.

quiz.q: A trader is long a call and delta-hedges it continuously. What mainly makes this position profitable?
opts: Realised volatility turning out higher than the implied volatility paid
The stock price drifting steadily upward
Time passing with the stock price unchanged
Interest rates falling to zero
quiz.ex: A delta-hedged long option is long gamma and pays theta; it earns money when actual moves are larger than those priced in.

chapters.title: Volatility smile and surface
chapters.read: The volatility smile chapter of an options textbook and a vendor note on FX or equity vol surfaces: implied versus realised volatility, skew and smile shapes, term structure, and ATM / risk reversal / butterfly quoting.
chapters.produce: Take a set of option quotes across strikes and expiries (made-up but realistic), back out implied vols with your Black-Scholes code, and draw the smile per expiry and a simple surface table.

quiz.q: What is an option's implied volatility?
opts: The standard deviation of the stock's past daily returns
The volatility that makes the Black-Scholes price equal to the option's market price
The volatility forecast published by the exchange
The average volatility of all options on the same underlying
quiz.ex: Implied volatility is backed out from a market price; historical volatility is measured from past returns.

quiz.q: In equity index options, what is the typical shape of implied volatility across strikes?
opts: All strikes have the same implied volatility
High-strike (OTM call) options have the highest implied vols
Low-strike (OTM put) options have higher implied vols than high-strike options
Implied vol is highest exactly at-the-money and falls on both sides
quiz.ex: Demand for crash protection and fatter left tails push up implied vols for low strikes: the equity skew.

quiz.q: A volatility surface shows implied volatility as a function of which two variables?
opts: Spot price and interest rate
Notional and counterparty rating
Trade date and settlement date
Strike (or delta) and time to expiry
quiz.ex: Each point on the surface is the implied vol for one strike/delta and one expiry.

quiz.q: In FX option markets, what does the 25-delta risk reversal mainly measure?
opts: The skew: whether calls or puts of the same delta are priced at higher vol
The overall level of at-the-money volatility
The curvature (smile wings) relative to ATM
The interest rate differential between the two currencies
quiz.ex: Risk reversal = vol(25Δ call) − vol(25Δ put); its sign shows which side is in demand. Curvature is the butterfly.

quiz.q: 25-delta call vol is 10.5% and 25-delta put vol is 12.0%. What is the 25-delta risk reversal (call minus put), in vol points?
quiz.ex: RR = 10.5 − 12.0 = −1.5 vol points: puts are bid.

quiz.q: Same quotes, ATM vol 10.8%. Using the simple formula butterfly = average of the 25-delta call and put vols minus ATM, what is the butterfly in vol points?

chapters.title: Market risk: DV01, VaR and stress tests
chapters.read: A risk management textbook's chapters on sensitivities and VaR: duration and DV01, parametric (variance-covariance) VaR, historical simulation, expected shortfall, square-root-of-time scaling, backtesting, and stress scenario design.
chapters.produce: Using two years of made-up daily P&L for a small portfolio, compute parametric and historical 1-day 99% VaR and 97.5% expected shortfall, then write a half-page stress test with three named scenarios.

quiz.q: A 10-year zero-coupon bond has face value ¥100,000,000 and a yield of 1% (annual compounding). Using modified duration, what is its DV01 (price change for a 1bp yield move)?
A ¥500m equity position has daily return volatility of 1.2%. Using z = 2.33, what is the 1-day 99% parametric VaR?
Scale that 1-day VaR of ¥13,980,000 to a 10-day horizon using the square-root-of-time rule.
A desk has 100 daily P&L scenarios. Its convention takes 99% historical VaR as the 2nd-largest loss. The five largest losses (¥m) are 12.4, 9.8, 8.1, 7.7, 6.0. What is the VaR in ¥m?
quiz.ex: Sort losses from largest: 12.4 is 1st, 9.8 is 2nd, so VaR = ¥9.8m.

quiz.q: Two desks have standalone parametric VaRs of ¥10m and ¥6m with correlation 0.3. What is the combined VaR in ¥m?
quiz.ex: VaR = √(10² + 6² + 2×0.3×10×6) = √172 ≈ ¥13.11m, less than 16 due to diversification.

quiz.q: What does a stress test add that VaR does not?
opts: It gives the exact probability of the worst loss
It shows the loss under specific severe scenarios, including ones beyond VaR's confidence level or outside the historical window
It replaces the need to compute sensitivities such as DV01
It measures average daily P&L under normal conditions
quiz.ex: VaR says little about the tail beyond its quantile; stress tests ask 'what if' about named extreme events.

chapters.title: Counterparty risk, CVA and XVA
chapters.read: A counterparty credit risk textbook's chapters on exposure (current, expected and potential future exposure), netting and collateral (ISDA/CSA), CVA as expected loss from counterparty default, and the wider XVA family: DVA, FVA, MVA, KVA.
chapters.produce: For a 5-year swap, take an assumed expected exposure profile and a flat credit spread, compute CVA in a spreadsheet, then show how it changes with netting and with a collateral agreement.

quiz.q: You have three trades with one counterparty, marked at +¥12m, −¥5m and +¥3m, all under one ISDA netting agreement. What is the current exposure in ¥m?
quiz.ex: With netting, exposure = max(12 − 5 + 3, 0) = ¥10m.

quiz.q: Same three trades (+12, −5, +3 ¥m) but with NO netting agreement. What is the current exposure in ¥m?
quiz.ex: Without netting, each trade counts separately: max(12,0) + max(−5,0) + max(3,0) = ¥15m.

quiz.q: Simple CVA: LGD 60%. Year 1: expected exposure ¥10m, default probability 2%, DF 0.98. Year 2: EE ¥8m, default probability 2%, DF 0.96. What is CVA in ¥m? (3 decimals)
A counterparty's CDS spread is 120bp and assumed recovery is 40%. Using the approximation λ ≈ spread / (1 − R), what is the annual default intensity in %?
What does DVA (debit valuation adjustment) reflect?
opts: The cost of funding uncollateralised positions
The cost of holding regulatory capital over the trade's life
The value to the bank of its own possible default on what it owes the counterparty
The counterparty's expected loss from the bank's collateral
quiz.ex: DVA is the mirror of CVA: it is the counterparty's CVA on the bank, a benefit in the bank's valuation.

quiz.q: Which XVA captures the cost of funding the initial margin a bank must post?
opts: CVA
KVA
DVA
MVA
quiz.ex: MVA (margin valuation adjustment) is the funding cost of initial margin; KVA is the cost of capital, CVA/DVA are credit adjustments.

chapters.title: Regulation basics: Basel, FRTB and trade reporting
chapters.read: An introductory overview of bank regulation from a regulator's or consultancy's explainer: the Basel three pillars, risk-weighted assets and capital ratios, FRTB's standardised and internal-model approaches, central clearing, and OTC derivatives trade reporting.
chapters.produce: Write a one-page memo for a markets-systems client explaining which data a trading platform must produce for FRTB sensitivities and for trade reporting, and which teams own each.

quiz.q: Under the Basel framework, what is Pillar 3 about?
opts: Public disclosure, so that market participants can judge a bank's risk and capital
Minimum capital requirements calculated from risk-weighted assets
Supervisory review of a bank's own risk and capital assessment
Deposit insurance for retail customers
quiz.ex: Pillar 1 is minimum capital, Pillar 2 is supervisory review, Pillar 3 is market discipline through disclosure.

quiz.q: For internal models, which risk measure does FRTB use in place of the older VaR-based market risk charge?
opts: Duration
Expected shortfall
Credit valuation adjustment
Liquidity coverage ratio
quiz.ex: FRTB moved internal models from VaR to expected shortfall, which captures the size of tail losses.

quiz.q: FRTB tightened the boundary between which two areas?
opts: The front office and the middle office
Retail and corporate lending
The trading book and the banking book
Spot and forward FX trades
quiz.ex: Stricter boundary rules limit banks moving positions between books to reduce capital.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of OTC derivatives trade reporting to trade repositories?
opts: To set the price at which trades are executed
To replace bilateral confirmations between counterparties
To calculate each bank's tax on derivatives
To give regulators visibility of positions and exposures across the market
quiz.ex: After 2008, regulators lacked a view of who held which OTC exposures; reporting gives them that data.

quiz.q: What does a central counterparty (CCP) do in a cleared derivative?
opts: It becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer, collecting margin from both
It acts only as a broker that finds a counterparty
It reports the trade but takes no risk
It guarantees the trade's profit for both sides
quiz.ex: Through novation the CCP stands between the parties and manages default risk with margin and a default fund.

quiz.q: A bank has CET1 capital of ¥8bn and risk-weighted assets of ¥100bn. What is its CET1 ratio in %?
quiz.ex: CET1 ratio = 8 / 100 = 8%.

boss.q: DF1 = 0.97 and DF2 = 0.94. The 3-year par swap rate (annual fixed) is 3.5%. Bootstrap DF3. (4 decimals)
DF1 0.97, DF2 0.94, DF3 0.91. What is the par rate of a 2-year swap starting in 1 year (annual fixed on years 2 and 3), in %?
Black-Scholes European put: S = 50, K = 55, r = 2% (continuous), σ = 30%, T = 0.5, no dividends. Price? (2 decimals)
You are long 2,000 listed put contracts (multiplier 100 shares) with delta −0.35 each. How many shares must you BUY to be delta-neutral?
Historical simulation with 200 scenarios. 97.5% expected shortfall is taken as the average of the 5 worst losses: 15, 12, 11, 9, 8 (¥m). What is ES in ¥m?
USD/JPY spot 150.00, 1-year forward 145.00, 1-year USD rate 4.5% simple. What 1-year JPY simple rate does covered interest parity imply, in %?
Annual DFs: 0.98, 0.955, 0.93, 0.90 (years 1–4). What is the value to the fixed-rate RECEIVER of a 4-year ¥2bn swap with 2.5% annual fixed rate?
Delta-normal VaR: long 1,000 calls (1 share each), delta 0.6, share price ¥2,000, daily vol 1.5%. Using z = 2.33, what is the 1-day 99% VaR?
Which situation is an example of wrong-way risk?
opts: A diversified portfolio of swaps with many unrelated counterparties
Buying credit protection on a Japanese bank from another Japanese bank whose credit is closely tied to it
A fully collateralised swap with daily margin calls
Receiving fixed on a swap when rates are expected to stay flat
boss.ex: Wrong-way risk is when exposure to a counterparty rises exactly as its default becomes more likely, as when the protection seller is hit by the same event.

boss.q: A trader prices a deep out-of-the-money equity index put using the at-the-money implied volatility. Given a typical equity skew, what happens?
opts: The put is overpriced, because low strikes trade at lower vol
The price is correct, because implied vol does not depend on strike
The put is underpriced, because low-strike options trade at higher implied vol than ATM
The error only affects calls, not puts
boss.ex: Equity skew means OTM puts carry higher implied vol; using the lower ATM vol gives too low a price.
